P3L1-L2 Assessment: Historical Data and Motion Analysis

Time: 45 minutes
Instructions: Answer all questions completely. Show all work for calculations. Use data from graphs and tables to support your reasoning.

Question 1 (5 points)

A traffic safety engineer notices that pedestrian fatalities have increased in urban areas over the past decade, despite overall vehicle safety improvements.

a) Select TWO possible explanations NOT related to vehicle design: (4 points)

  • A) Vehicles have become less safe
  • B) Increased use of smartphones while walking
  • C) More pedestrians in urban areas due to population growth
  • D) Vehicles are traveling faster
  • E) Improved emergency medical response
  • F) Better road lighting

b) To test these explanations, which data would be MOST useful? (2 points)

  • A) Vehicle sales figures
  • B) Pedestrian smartphone usage and foot traffic patterns
  • C) Weather data
  • D) Gas prices over time

c) How can understanding historical safety trends help engineers design better systems? (2 points)

  • A) It provides entertainment value
  • B) It identifies which past solutions worked and failed
  • C) It predicts exact future outcomes
  • D) It reduces the need for new testing

Part B: Motion Analysis and Position-Time Graphs (25 points)

Question 4 (12 points)

A driver education instructor tests student reaction times. The position-time graph below shows a car during emergency braking:

a) Calculate the reaction distance. Show your work. (3 points)

Reaction distance = ___ meters

b) Calculate the braking distance. Show your work. (3 points)

Braking distance = ___ meters

c) Calculate the car’s velocity during reaction time. Show your work. (3 points)

Velocity = ___ m/s

d) Why is the line from A to B straight while B to D is curved? (3 points)

  • A) The car was broken during braking
  • B) During reaction time velocity is constant; during braking velocity decreases
  • C) The driver was accelerating, then decelerating
  • D) The graph is drawn incorrectly

Question 5 (8 points)

Two students conducted the same braking experiment. Student A was focused; Student B was texting.

a) Based on the graphs, which student had the longer total stopping distance? (4 points)

  • A) Student A (focused driver)
  • B) Student B (distracted driver)
  • C) Both had the same stopping distance
  • D) Cannot be determined from the graph

b) Explain why distraction affects stopping distance using physics concepts: (4 points)

  • A) Distraction makes brakes work poorly
  • B) Distraction increases reaction time, so the car travels farther at constant speed before braking begins
  • C) Distracted drivers brake harder
  • D) Distraction only affects steering, not stopping

Question 6 (5 points)

Position-time graph interpretation:

a) When velocity is constant on a P-T graph, the line appears: (2 points)

  • A) Curved upward
  • B) Curved downward
  • C) Straight and sloped
  • D) Horizontal (flat)

b) When velocity is decreasing on a P-T graph, the line appears: (2 points)

  • A) Curved with decreasing slope
  • B) Straight with constant slope
  • C) Horizontal
  • D) Vertical

c) A horizontal line on a P-T graph indicates: (1 point)

  • A) Constant velocity
  • B) The object is not moving (velocity = 0)
  • C) Increasing velocity
  • D) Decreasing velocity

Part C: Connecting Concepts (15 points)

Question 7 (8 points)

Modern vehicle safety features and their physics applications:

a) How would Anti-lock Braking Systems (ABS) most likely affect the braking portion of a position-time graph? (3 points)

  • A) Make the braking line perfectly straight
  • B) Allow for more controlled deceleration, potentially reducing braking distance
  • C) Increase the braking time significantly
  • D) Have no effect on the graph

b) Automatic emergency braking systems detect obstacles and brake faster than human reaction time. This technology would: (3 points)

  • A) Only affect the braking distance
  • B) Reduce the reaction distance portion of stopping distance
  • C) Increase total stopping distance
  • D) Only work at high speeds

c) How could P-T graphs help engineers design collision avoidance systems? (2 points)

  • A) They show pretty pictures of motion
  • B) They help calculate minimum safe distances and required reaction times
  • C) They are required by law
  • D) They predict weather conditions

Question 8 (7 points)

Research design for studying distracted driving:

a) To study how different distractions affect reaction time, identify: (3 points)

Independent variable:

  • A) Age of driver
  • B) Type of distraction (texting, talking, etc.)
  • C) Reaction time measured
  • D) Weather conditions

Dependent variable:

  • A) Type of distraction
  • B) Time of day
  • C) Reaction time measured
  • D) Vehicle type

b) Position-time graphs could analyze this data by: (2 points)

  • A) Showing how reaction distance changes with different distractions
  • B) Predicting future accidents
  • C) Measuring vehicle speeds only
  • D) Calculating fuel efficiency

c) An important ethical consideration for this research would be: (2 points)

  • A) Using the fastest cars available
  • B) Ensuring participant safety during controlled testing
  • C) Testing only professional drivers
  • D) Conducting tests during rush hour

Part D: Mathematical Application (10 points)

Question 9 (10 points)

A driver traveling at 25 m/s (about 56 mph) sees an obstacle ahead.

Given:

  • Initial speed: 25 m/s
  • Reaction time: 1.2 seconds
  • Braking deceleration: 8 m/s² (constant)
  • Time to stop after braking begins: 3.1 seconds

a) Calculate the reaction distance. (2 points)

Reaction distance = speed × time = ___ meters

b) Calculate the braking distance using: distance = initial velocity × time + ½ × acceleration × time² (Note: acceleration is negative for braking) (4 points)

Braking distance = ___ meters

c) Calculate the total stopping distance. (2 points)

Total stopping distance = ___ meters

d) If the obstacle was 75 meters away when first spotted, will the driver avoid collision? (2 points)

  • A) Yes, stopping distance is less than 75 meters
  • B) No, stopping distance exceeds 75 meters
  • C) Exactly equal - will barely stop in time
  • D) Cannot determine from given information

Show reasoning: _____________

Answer Key

Part A

  1. a) C b) Period 1: C, Period 2: B c) B
  2. a) 1925: 0.001095 fatalities/vehicle; 2020: 0.000138 fatalities/vehicle b) B c) A, B, C, F
  3. a) B, C b) B c) B

Part B

  1. a) 30 meters b) 50 meters c) 20 m/s d) B
  2. a) B b) B
  3. a) C b) A c) B

Part C

  1. a) B b) B c) B
  2. a) Independent: B, Dependent: C b) A c) B

Part D

  1. a) 30 meters b) 38.5 meters c) 68.5 meters d) B (total > 75m, collision will occur)

Required AI-Generated Figures Summary

  1. Historical fatality rates line graph (1920-2020)
  2. Transportation safety data table (1925 vs 2020 comparison)
  3. Emergency braking P-T graph (single scenario with labeled points)
  4. Comparison P-T graphs (focused vs distracted driver on same axes)

Each figure should be generated using Python matplotlib with clear labels, appropriate scales, and professional formatting suitable for a physics assessment.

Scoring Rubric

Part A - Historical Data Analysis (25 points)

  • Exemplary (23-25): Accurately interprets trends, provides detailed explanations with evidence, makes sophisticated connections between data and safety factors
  • Proficient (18-22): Correctly interprets most trends, provides reasonable explanations, makes basic connections
  • Developing (13-17): Some accurate interpretation, explanations lack detail or evidence
  • Beginning (0-12): Limited accuracy in interpretation, minimal explanations

Part B - Motion Analysis (25 points)

  • Exemplary (23-25): Accurate calculations with proper units, clear understanding of P-T graphs, sophisticated explanations
  • Proficient (18-22): Most calculations correct, good understanding of graphs, adequate explanations
  • Developing (13-17): Some calculation errors, basic understanding of graphs
  • Beginning (0-12): Significant calculation errors, limited graph interpretation

Part C - Connecting Concepts (15 points)

  • Exemplary (14-15): Makes sophisticated connections between physics and technology, demonstrates deep understanding
  • Proficient (11-13): Makes appropriate connections, shows good understanding
  • Developing (8-10): Makes basic connections, shows developing understanding
  • Beginning (0-7): Limited connections, minimal understanding

Part D - Mathematical Application (10 points)

  • Exemplary (9-10): All calculations correct with proper units and clear reasoning
  • Proficient (7-8): Most calculations correct with minor errors
  • Developing (5-6): Some calculation errors but shows understanding of process
  • Beginning (0-4): Significant calculation errors, limited understanding

Overall Grade Scale:

  • A: 68-75 points (91-100%)
  • B: 60-67 points (80-90%)
  • C: 53-59 points (70-79%)
  • D: 45-52 points (60-69%)
  • F: Below 45 points (<60%)

NGSS Alignment

Performance Expectations:

  • ETS1.A: Defining and Delimiting Engineering Problems - Criteria and constraints for solutions

Science and Engineering Practices (SEPs):

  • Analyzing and Interpreting Data
  • Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking
  • Constructing Explanations and Designing Solutions

Crosscutting Concepts (CCCs):

  • Patterns in historical safety data
  • Cause and Effect relationships between technology and safety
  • Systems and System Models in transportation safety
